extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in classical/analytic geometry (readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Determine the species (ellipse / hyperbola / parabola) of the section produced when a plane cuts a second-degree surface; compute volumes and centroids of solid sectors formed by a surface and the cone with vertex at the origin; and related classical results (continued-fraction convergents, assorted geometry problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species criterion (AC − B²) for plane sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The curve in which the surface of the second degree (general quadratic in x,y,z) is cut by a plane (with normal directing cosines l,m,n) is an ellipse, a hyperbola, or a parabola according as AC − B² is positive, negative, or zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The section equation (after reducing coordinates so the plane's normal aligns with a coordinate axis) has form A y'² + 2B y' z' + C z'² + ... = 0 and the decisive quantity is AC − B². A, B, C are combinations of the original quadratic coefficients P₁,P₂,P₃ and the directing cosines l,m,n: e.g. A = P₁ l'² + P₂ m'² + P₃ n'², etc. Use this sign test to classify any plane section. (Original text: 'Now according as AC − B’ is positive, negative, or zero, the section (6) will be an ellipse, an hyperbola, or a parabola; and hence The curve in which the surface (1) is cut by the plane (2) will be an ellipse, an hyperbola, or a parabola, according as (8) is positive, negative, or zero.')

rubrics_metrics.name: General quadratic-form criterion (formula (10))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface given under the general quadratic form (nine independent coefficients) and a cutting plane La + My + Nz = P', the species of the section is determined by the sign of a particular combination of coefficients (formula (10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula (10) is the explicit criterion involving the quadratic-form coefficients Aᵢ, Bᵢ, Cᵢ and the plane coefficients L,M,N: its sign (positive/negative/zero) determines ellipse/hyperbola/parabola. Use this when the surface is presented in the general quadratic form rather than the diagonalized P₁,P₂,P₃ form. (Original text: 'If the equation to the surface be given under the general form ... the species of the section made by any plane (2) may still be ascertained. ... the criterion here is (10), hence the section will be an ellipse, an hyperbola, or a parabola, according as (10) is positive, negative, or zero.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow using non-normalized plane coefficients (L,M,N proportional to directing cosines)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cutting plane is given by La + My + Nz = P' where L,M,N are not the directing cosines, one may use L,M,N (proportional to  l,m,n) in the classification criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because l,m,n are proportional to L,M,N, substitute L,M,N into the sign-criteria expressions (8) or (10) instead of normalizing to unit-length cosines. (Original text: 'Note.—Though the criteria (8) and (10) have been here established only when the axes are rectangular, they are nevertheless true when the axes are oblique;  l,m,n continuing to be the cosines of the angles which the normal to the cutting plane makes with the axes, and for l,m,n we may, as above, substitute the coefficients L,M,N of a,y,z in the equation La + My + Nz = P' of this plane.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Central-surface corollary: ellipsoid sections
rubrics_metrics.description: For central surfaces (ellipsoid) where P₁,P₂,P₃ are all positive, the decisive quantity (AC − B²) is always positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore every plane section of an ellipsoid is an ellipse. (Original text: 'In the central surfaces P₁,P₂,P₃ are all different from zero, and for an ellipsoid they are all positive,—hence (8) being always positive and never = 0*, all the sections are ellipses.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloid/cone corollary: all section species possible
rubrics_metrics.description: For the two hyperboloids and the cone (coefficients Pᵢ of mixed signs), the discriminant AC − B² may be positive, negative, or zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus such surfaces can be cut by a plane to yield an ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola depending on plane orientation. (Original text: 'For the two hyperboloids and the cone, either one ... or two ... of the coefficients P₁,P₂,P₃ are negative, and hence ... (8) may be either positive, negative, or zero; consequently any of these surfaces may be cut by a plane in either an ellipse, an hyperbola, or a parabola.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraboloid / elliptic-hyperbolic cylinder criterion (one coefficient zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one (and only one) of P₁,P₂,P₃ is zero (paraboloids or certain cylinders), reduce (8) accordingly; its sign determines the section type and planes parallel to the axis give parabolas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If P₁ = 0 then (8) reduces to (8') involving only the remaining coefficients; if those remaining have same sign, (8') positive (ellipse), if opposite sign, (8') negative (hyperbola), and when certain directional cosines vanish the expression may be zero (parabola). In particular, every plane parallel to the axis of the z (the axis corresponding to the zero coefficient) yields a parabola. (Original text summarised from 'With respect to the paraboloids and the elliptic and hyperbolic cylinders, one (and one only) of the coefficients P₁,P₂,P₃ is zero... Now if P₂,P₃ have the same sign, (8') will be positive, but if different signs it will be negative, except l=0, in which case (8') will vanish. Hence every section ... made by a plane parallel to the axis of z is a parabola.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic-cylinder corollary (two coefficients zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two of the coefficients P₁,P₂,P₃ are zero (parabolic cylinder), the classification expression vanishes and plane sections are parabolas or a pair of parallel lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All plane sections of a parabolic cylinder are parabolas (or the degenerate case of two parallel lines). (Original text: 'The only remaining surface of the second degree is the parabolic cylinder, for which two of the coefficients P₁, P₂, P₃ are zero; hence (7) will always vanish, and the plane sections are all parabolas, or a system of two parallel straight lines.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of solid sector via tangent-plane linearization
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface z = f(x,y), form the conical solid with vertex at origin and base the given closed curve on the surface; if p = ∂z/∂x and q = ∂z/∂y at a point, the elemental cone volume integrates to give V = (1/3) ∫(z − p x − q y) dx dy over the projection of the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The integration must extend over all elements da dy of the projection. Crucially, z − p x − q y must not change sign within the limits of integration (otherwise P would change sign and the formula fails); if it does, divide the base into parts where the sign is constant and sum their volumes. The derivation uses the tangent plane equation and the cone-volume formula. (Original text: 'If V denote the volume ... it is required to show that V = +3//(z − p a − q y) da dy ... It must be observed that in (6), z − p a − q y ought not to change sign within the limits of integration ... In this case we may divide the base, and consequently the sector, into two such parts that (6) may be applicable to each, and the sum of the volumes of the two parts will determine the whole volume.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Centroid formulae for the solid sector (from elemental cones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the elemental cones (whose centroids are determined from geometry of cones), the moments of the sector are integrals of x(z − p x − q y), y(z − p x − q y), z(z − p x − q y) over the projection, giving V·x̄, V·ȳ, V·z̄.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text derives V·x = (1/4) ∫ x (z − p x − q y) dx dy etc. (presentation is via the elemental cone centroid and integration). Apply same sign requirement as for volume; if z − p x − q y changes sign, split the region. (Original text: 'Again, the centre of gravity of the elemental cone ... and hence we have V.a = 2/26V, ete.; (5) V.2 = th/fa(z — p e — q y) da dy ... and Viz =k isf xz — p e — q y) da dy }' — i.e. the centroid components are proportional integrals of x,y,z times (z − p x − q y).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar-coordinates method for volume & centroid
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the volume and centroid by integrating in spherical (polar) coordinates: if r(φ,θ) gives radial limit, then V = ∫(1/3) r³ sin θ dθ dφ and the moments are ∫(1/4) r⁴ times trig factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ and integrate r from 0 to r(φ,θ), θ between 0 and F(φ), φ between 0 and 2π (or as limited). Then Vx,Vy,Vz follow by multiplying by appropriate cos/sin factors and integrating. The text notes the practical advice to eliminate y via the plane-projection relation when performing integrations in the order θ then φ. (Original text paraphrase: 'Let (ρ, θ, φ) denote the polar coordinates ... V = ∫∫ ρ³ sin θ dρ dθ dφ, integrating ρ between 0 and r gives V = ∫∫ (1/3) r³ sin θ dθ dφ ... Also Vx = ∫∫ (1/4) r⁴ sin³ θ cos φ dθ dφ, etc. ... the integration must be performed, first with respect to θ, between limits 0 and F(φ), then with respect to φ between 0 and 2π.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering/selection rules for secondary convergents of continued fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three consecutive principal convergents and the quotient g, construct secondary convergents; the first half of these secondary fractions (excluding the middle when the number is odd) are nearer to the true value than the simpler principal convergent, while the second half are farther; the middle one (if present) must be decided by comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page proves that ordering principal and secondary convergents by denominator yields a series in which each fraction approximates the value more closely than any other fraction with smaller denominator. The practical rule: when inserting secondaries between principal convergents, keep those whose index lies in the first half (except certain equalities); decide the middle secondary by explicit inequality checks (compare cross-products or derived inequalities). The theorem is illustrated with examples and a worked continued-fraction expansion. (Original text: 'Hence we see that in all cases, the first half of the secondary fractions (leaving out the middle one when their number is odd) will be nearer to, and the second half farther from the true value of the whole fraction than the simpler principal convergent — ... As to the middle secondary when the number is odd it being more or less approximative than - depends ...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecutive convergents cross-multiplication property
rubrics_metrics.description: For the constructed series of principal and kept secondary convergents ordered by denominator, the numerators and denominators of any two consecutive fractions, when cross-multiplied (m·Q' − n·Q), give results differing by unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property is used in proofs of uniqueness/optimality of the convergent series: it also holds for the last fraction of one set and any fraction of the following set. Use this to argue minimality of approximation for given denominator bound. (Original text: 'It follows evidently from what precedes, that the numerator and denominator of any two consecutive fractions, cross multiplied, will give results differing by unity, and that this property holds for the last fraction of one set and any one of the fractions of the following set.')
